entry: argument-from-ignorance LA2 (procedural default) + METHOD (b) "treat stated defaults as such"
fix: LA2 applies only to a default established independently of this argument (law, regulation, a null hypothesis or house rule set beforehand), and only if the conclusion stays a decision and does not also assert the claim. Add: "if an established standard exists and points the other way, the speaker cannot replace it with their own default". Add a separate precautionary look-alike: "a cautious decision under uncertainty, stated as a decision, with costs weighed" (round-1 P069/P098). With this, Q012 -> flag (FCC limits are the established default and are conceded; "the responsible assumption is that it isn't [harmless]" asserts harm).
rationale: Both reviewers saw the fallacy (C: "my view: flag"), but LA2 let the speaker create a default just by calling it an "assumption". Key is right.

entry: base-rate-fallacy C2 outside-text; affirming-the-consequent C3 "definitely"; undistributed-middle LA1 exempts "likely"; inductive-conversion C2 only covers all/most B are A
fix: Add an entry, converse error (probabilistic affirming the consequent / confusing P(E|H) with P(H|E)), in the probability family. C1: the passage states that all/most H have feature E. C2: a case with E is concluded to be (probably) H. C3: no information on how common E is among non-H is given or used. All conditions are textual. Probability family tie-break: courtroom "chance if innocent" -> prosecutor's; test/screening with prevalence -> base rate; "all H have E; this has E; so (probably) H" -> converse error. Key: add base rate / converse error / inverse probability to the acceptable names. Undistributed middle is a poor fit for a "likely" conclusion; the key's own reason ("traits are also common among legitimate charities") describes base-rate neglect.
rationale: C applied the literal rules correctly and every entry failed. D flagged by treating "legit charities share these traits" as common knowledge. D's verdict is right; C exposed the gap.

entry: cherry-picking C2 "stated or plainly known"; selective-evidence tie-break; METHOD (b) common-knowledge threshold
fix: cherry-picking: add a chosen-window clause. C1 is met when "a measurement period is chosen while the arguer's own stated record extends beyond it". C2 is met when "a comparative claim (beats the market, best ever) is made with no comparison figure and the window excludes stated history". Define common knowledge in METHOD (b): "an educated general reader would know it without looking it up; if reviewers could reasonably differ, treat it as not common knowledge and record possible issue". With this, Q050 -> flag from the text alone ("since 2001" vs "measured from March 2009", and "beats the market" with no market figure), without needing to know the 2009 market low.
rationale: D's flag relied on March 2009 being "plainly known" as the market bottom. That is defensible, but it depends on the threshold. The text alone supports the flag once the window clause exists.

entry: no Simpson's paradox / aggregation entry; cherry-picking C1 "subset"
fix: Add an entry, Simpson's paradox (aggregation reversal), statistical family. C1: an aggregate comparison between groups is made. C2: data broken down by a factor (stated or plainly known) reverse or remove the difference. C3: the groups differ in composition on that factor. C4: the conclusion is drawn from the aggregate. Look-alike: the aggregate is the quantity actually relevant to the decision (for example, a patient who cannot know their risk stratum; still say so). Tie-break: strata data reverse the aggregate -> Simpson's; a third factor merely unaddressed -> common cause.
rationale: The aggregate isn't a "subset", so cherry-picking is a forced fit. D's common-cause (confounding by case mix) is acceptable under the key ("confounding").

entry: causation family rule ("only a correlation is shown: cum hoc" vs "addresses causes but misses an obvious third factor: common cause"); cum-hoc C2/C3 and common-cause C1 assume an explicit causal claim
fix: METHOD (b): "a recommendation whose only rationale is a causal effect counts as asserting that effect, and as established unless hedged" (also fixes Q008). Rewrite the causation tie-break to key on the most specific alternative: an obvious third factor that is named or plainly known (including the reason cases were selected into the group, such as sicker patients being referred) -> common cause; a plausible reverse direction -> reversing causation; no specific alternative identifiable -> cum hoc; observational-interpretation only when a study is cited as showing causation and the problem is the design itself. Key: the reason "causation runs the other way" is better described as confounding by indication (severity causes both referral and death); keep "reverse causation" acceptable, but add common cause.
rationale: Both labels are acceptable, but the split is arbitrary. C used cum hoc because nothing was adjusted; D used common cause because severity is obvious. The tie-break keys on what the argument does, when it should key on which alternative is identifiable.

entry: appeal-to-nature C1 trigger ("what our bodies are built for") vs LA2 ("evolutionary history as evidence of physiological fit"); no cross-family tie-break nature vs tradition
fix: appeal-to-nature LA2: require "independent physiological evidence of fit (digestion, nutrient data), not merely a long history of use or the phrase itself". Add a cross-family tie-break: wording about what is natural or what bodies are built for -> appeal to nature; age or history only -> appeal to tradition; if one sentence does both for one conclusion, it is one step: report appeal to nature and note tradition.
rationale: Both labels are in the key. C avoided appeal to nature only because LA2 seemed to exempt its own trigger wording.

entry: complex-question C2 (not marked outside-text) and LA1; avoiding-the-question LA2 points back to complex-question
fix: Key: re-grade the target to possible issue. Whether enforcement stopped is an outside fact; complaints about smell don't establish it; "four inspections" doesn't rebut it either (inspection is not enforcement action), so the questioner or the commissioner could be the one at fault. Catalog: mark complex-question C2 as outside-text and reword it to "contested and not established in the passage". Avoiding-the-question LA2 applies only if the respondent actually says the presupposition is false. Add a tie-break: if the answer implicitly disputes the presupposition with a relevant fact and the record is not in the text -> possible issue under complex question, settled by the enforcement record.
row_type: soft miss vs key (both) - key overruled
rationale: Both reviewers gave the right answer for a text-only method. The key assumes facts the passage doesn't give.

entry: METHOD has no record for non-fallacy errors
fix: Key: correct the reason. The inverse-variance mean of 4.2+/-0.9 and 5.8+/-0.6 is 5.31%, and the simple midpoint is 5.0% (not 5.3%). The passage's 5.1% is an arithmetic error. Either fix the passage to 5.3% or keep it as a planted non-fallacy error. METHOD: add an optional "other errors (not fallacies)" field for arithmetic and factual slips, recorded without a fallacy label and without changing the verdict.
rationale: Both reviewers independently caught the arithmetic (C and D notes). The key reason has the midpoint wrong and misses the passage's error.

entry: no statistical-vs-practical-significance entry
fix: Add an entry, statistical vs practical significance. C1: a result is reported as statistically significant. C2: it is presented as large, important or worth acting on. C3: the effect size stated (or omitted) does not support that. Tie-break: the word "significant" shifts senses -> may also be equivocation; report the new entry.
rationale: Caught only because the word "significant" appears twice.

entry: no relative-vs-absolute-risk entry
fix: Add an entry, relative risk framing. C1: a relative change is reported. C2: the absolute change is small, stated or omitted. C3: the conclusion relies on the relative figure as if it were large. Look-alike: both figures given and weighed.
rationale: Caught only because the bleeding rate was on the page. "50% reduction!" alone would have no entry.

entry: affirming-the-consequent C3 "definitely"; denying-the-antecedent C3 (Q033)
fix: AC C3: "P is concluded as following (certain or near-certain), or as probable with no other explanation considered". Mirror this in DA C3 for hedged not-Q conclusions (Q033 "shouldn't count on her").
rationale: Both flagged by treating "hard to avoid the conclusion" as near-certain.

rationale: The hundred-year-flood form is the mirror image of the wording.
